summary:
Astronix Core is an interactive astronaut health monitoring prototype that brings simulated health indicators, trends, and alerts into one browser dashboard. It displays heart rate, accumulated radiation dose, relative bone density, stress, hydration, and metabolism, alongside an interactive body map.

Users can explore five mission scenarios, including low Earth orbit, lunar surface activity, a solar particle event, extended Mars transit, and atmospheric re-entry. Adjusting radiation rate, mission duration, or stress immediately updates the indicators, charts, and prioritized alerts.

The project addresses the challenge by demonstrating how health information can help crew members recognize changes and identify issues requiring attention. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Chart.js, it offers an accessible platform for education and interface exploration. All readings, physiological relationships, and alert thresholds are illustrative; the prototype does not provide medical diagnoses or use live astronaut telemetry.
details:
Astronix Core demonstrates an interactive workflow for monitoring astronaut health: view indicators, explore trends, locate areas of concern, and review prioritized alerts.

The dashboard combines four primary indicators—heart rate, accumulated radiation dose, relative bone density, and stress - with radiation, hydration, and metabolism charts. An interactive body map displays illustrative regional load, temperature, and status information.

Five presets represent different mission conditions: nominal low Earth orbit, lunar surface extravehicular activity, a solar particle event, extended Mars transit, and atmospheric re-entry. Users can adjust radiation rate, mission duration, and physiological stress. A shared JavaScript simulation model recalculates the indicators and updates the dashboard every second.

Accumulated radiation dose is calculated from the selected daily dose rate and elapsed mission duration. Other indicators use simplified relationships that demonstrate how mission duration, physical workload, and stress can affect the displayed state. These relationships are illustrative rather than validated physiological predictions.

A rule-based alert engine evaluates the simulated indicators, sorts alerts by severity, and displays suggested topics for review, including shielding, workload, exercise, hydration, and recovery. Users can acknowledge alerts, and an event log records status changes. Acknowledgement does not perform any medical action.

The prototype uses HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, and Chart.js. It runs in the browser without a backend or specialized hardware; charts and fonts are loaded from external services.

Its creative contribution is the combination of scenario controls, coordinated health indicators, an interactive body map, and explanatory alerts in a single interface. The intended benefit is to make relationships between mission conditions and health indicators easier to explore and understand.

In preparing the scientific context for this submission, we consulted NASA Human Research Program resources on the five hazards and risks of human spaceflight. These resources provide background on radiation, altered gravity, isolation, and physiological and behavioral risks. No NASA astronaut records or research datasets were imported, and the numerical coefficients and alert thresholds are not NASA medical limits.

This is an educational and interface demonstration. Future development would require validated models, integration with actual sensors, individualized baselines, and evaluation with medical and human-factors specialists before operational use.
